topics.title: Rome: from Republic to Empire
topics.intro: Rome began, legend says, in 753 BC. Its people threw out their kings and ran a republic for nearly 500 years, until ambitious generals with loyal armies turned it into an empire.
topics.teach: Explain why the Roman Republic became an empire.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which Greek gods the Romans renamed, and what they called Athena.
topics.hook: Kings, then a Republic (**509 BC**), then an Empire (**27 BC**): Rome tried three kinds of government in turn.

topics.title: The Crusades
topics.intro: In 1095 the Pope called on Christians to march to the Holy Land and take Jerusalem. For two centuries crusades brought war, faith, trade and terrible violence to the Middle East and to Europe.
topics.teach: Explain two different reasons why people joined the First Crusade.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what {she} thinks of Saladin and Richard the Lionheart, and why.
topics.hook: **1095** called, **1099** captured, **1187** lost again: the First Crusade and its undoing.

topics.title: The Wars of the Roses
topics.intro: From 1455 to 1487 the royal families of Lancaster and York fought for the English crown. It ended at Bosworth in 1485 with a new dynasty: the Tudors.
topics.teach: Explain why Henry Tudor won the Battle of Bosworth.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what {she} thinks happened to the Princes in the Tower, and what evidence {she} would want.
topics.hook: **Red** rose for Lancaster, **white** rose for York, joined in the **Tudor** rose after Bosworth in 1485.

topics.title: The Renaissance and the printing press
topics.intro: In fifteenth-century Italy, artists and scholars rediscovered Greek and Roman learning. Meanwhile a German goldsmith’s printing press let ideas spread faster than ever before.
topics.teach: Explain how the printing press helped new ideas spread.
topics.talk: Look at a Renaissance painting together and ask {him} how it differs from medieval art.
topics.hook: **Re-naissance** = rebirth: Greek and Roman ideas born again in Florence, then spread by Gutenberg’s press.

topics.title: The age of exploration
topics.intro: From the 1490s European sailors crossed oceans to the Americas, round Africa to India and right round the world. It brought new knowledge and trade, and conquest, disease and enslavement for millions.
topics.teach: Explain one positive and one terrible consequence of European exploration.
topics.talk: Ask {him} whether “discovery” is the right word for Columbus reaching the Caribbean.
topics.hook: Columbus went west (**1492**), da Gama went east (**1498**), Magellan and Elcano went right round (**1519–22**).

topics.title: Elizabeth I: a golden age?
topics.intro: Elizabeth I reigned for 44 years, survived plots and a Spanish invasion fleet, and presided over Shakespeare’s England. But was it really a golden age, and for whom?
topics.teach: Explain why Mary, Queen of Scots, was such a danger to Elizabeth.
topics.talk: Ask {him} why Elizabeth never married, in {her} opinion.
topics.hook: **1558–1603**: the Virgin Queen, also called Gloriana, reigned for 44 years.

topics.title: The Scientific Revolution
topics.intro: Between Copernicus in 1543 and Newton in 1687, thinkers replaced ancient authority with observation and experiment, and changed how we see the universe and our own bodies.
topics.teach: Explain why Galileo’s ideas alarmed the Church.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which scientist {she} would most like to meet, and what {she} would ask.
topics.hook: **1543 to 1687**: from Copernicus moving the Earth to Newton explaining why it moves.

topics.title: Restoration London: plague and fire
topics.intro: In 1660 the monarchy returned. Within six years London had suffered its last great plague and a fire that destroyed most of the old city, and began to rebuild in brick and stone.
topics.teach: Explain why the Great Fire spread so far.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what {she} would have buried in the garden, like Samuel Pepys.
topics.hook: King back in **1660**, plague in **1665**, fire in **1666**: two disasters in two years.

topics.title: The American Revolution
topics.intro: Thirteen British colonies in North America objected to taxes set by a Parliament they had no vote in. By 1783 they had won a war and their independence as the United States.
topics.teach: Explain what “no taxation without representation” meant.
topics.talk: Ask {him} whether the Declaration’s words “all men are created equal” were true in 1776.
topics.hook: “**No taxation without representation**”: the slogan that turned a quarrel over tax into a revolution.

topics.title: Napoleon and Georgian Britain
topics.intro: Out of the French Revolution came a brilliant general who made himself emperor and conquered much of Europe. Britain fought him at sea and on land for over a decade, while facing unrest at home.
topics.teach: Explain why Napoleon was eventually defeated.
topics.talk: Ask {him} why Nelson is on top of a column in Trafalgar Square.
topics.hook: **Trafalgar 1805** at sea, **Waterloo 1815** on land: Nelson, then Wellington.

topics.title: The Great Irish Famine
topics.intro: From 1845 a plant disease destroyed Ireland’s potato crop year after year. About a million people died and another million or more emigrated. How the government responded is still argued about today.
topics.teach: Explain why the potato blight caused a famine on such a scale.
topics.talk: Ask {him} why so many Americans and British people have Irish ancestors.
topics.hook: **1845 to 1851**: about a million died and over a million left; Ireland lost about a quarter of its people.

topics.title: Victorian cities and public health
topics.intro: Fast-growing industrial towns were crowded, filthy and deadly. Cholera, a doctor with a map, a summer stink and the germ theory finally pushed Parliament into cleaning them up.
topics.teach: Explain how John Snow showed that cholera spread through water.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what {she} would do first if {she} were in charge of a Victorian town.
topics.hook: **Snow’s map** (1854), the **Stink** (1858), Bazalgette’s **sewers**: evidence, then crisis, then action.

topics.title: Votes for women: the tactics
topics.intro: Suffragists and suffragettes wanted the same thing but argued fiercely about how to get it. Hunger strikes, window-smashing, a census boycott and war work all played a part, but which mattered most?
topics.teach: Explain the arguments for and against militant tactics.
topics.talk: Ask {him} whether breaking the law can ever be right to win a vote.
topics.hook: Suffra**gists** were gentle; suffra**gettes** got going with direct action. Same goal, different tactics.

topics.title: Britain’s Home Front, 1939–45
topics.intro: The Second World War was fought in Britain’s towns and kitchens as well as on battlefields: evacuation, rationing, the Blitz and women’s war work changed everyday life.
topics.teach: Explain how rationing worked and why it was needed.
topics.talk: Ask a grandparent what their family remembered about rationing or evacuation.
topics.hook: **Evacuate, ration, dig, shelter**: four verbs for life on the Home Front.

topics.title: Civil rights in the USA and Britain
topics.intro: After 1945 Black Americans and Black Britons campaigned against segregation and discrimination. Boycotts, marches and court cases won new laws, though the struggle for equality went on.
topics.teach: Explain why the Montgomery Bus Boycott was significant.
topics.talk: Ask {him} why Rosa Parks’ decision on one bus mattered so much.
topics.hook: **1954** schools, **1955** buses, **1963** the dream, **1964** the law: a decade that changed America.

topics.title: The end of empire
topics.intro: Within twenty-five years of 1945 most of Britain’s empire had become independent, beginning with India and Pakistan in 1947. Independence movements, war and money all played a part.
topics.teach: Explain why Gandhi’s methods were effective.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which countries in the Commonwealth {she} can name.
topics.hook: India and Pakistan in **1947**, Ghana in **1957**: ten years apart, as the empire began to unwind.

topics.title: Byzantium: the Roman Empire that spoke Greek
topics.intro: When the western Roman Empire fell in AD 476, the eastern half carried on for nearly a thousand years from Constantinople, speaking Greek and preserving ancient learning.
topics.teach: Explain how Byzantium helped to preserve Greek learning.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what Constantinople is called today.
topics.hook: **330** founded, **476** the West falls, **1453** Constantinople falls: the East lasted almost a thousand years longer.

topics.title: The Russian Revolutions of 1917
topics.intro: In 1917 Russia had two revolutions in a single year: first the Tsar fell, then Lenin’s Bolsheviks seized power. The world’s first communist state was born.
topics.teach: Explain why the Tsar lost power in February 1917.
topics.talk: Ask {him} why the “October” Revolution happened in November.
topics.hook: **February**: the Tsar falls. **October**: the Bolsheviks take over. Two revolutions in **1917**.

topics.title: The road to the Second World War
topics.intro: Between 1919 and 1939 a harsh peace treaty, a world economic depression and the rise of dictators in Italy, Germany and the USSR led the world back to war.
topics.teach: Explain what appeasement was and why Chamberlain chose it.
topics.talk: Ask {him} whether {she} thinks appeasement was cowardly or sensible.
topics.hook: **1919, 1929, 1933, 1938**: Versailles, Wall Street, Hitler, Munich: twenty years from war to war.

items.prompt: According to legend, which twin founded Rome in 753 BC?
items.explain: Legend says Romulus killed his brother Remus and named the city after himself. Historians treat the story as myth.
items.hook: **Legend** says Romulus and Remus were raised by a she-wolf, and Romulus named the city after himself.
items.example: The bronze she-wolf feeding the twins is still a symbol of the city of Rome.

items.prompt: What did the Romans do in about 509 BC?

options.text: They expelled their last king and set up a republic
They crowned their first emperor, Augustus
options.feedback: That was Augustus, nearly 500 years later.

options.text: They conquered Greece and its colonies
options.feedback: Greece came under Roman control in the 100s BC.

items.explain: The last king, Tarquin the Proud, was driven out. “Res publica” means “the public thing”: the state belonged to the people.
items.hook: **Res publica** = “the public thing”, which gives us the word **republic**.
items.example: France, Ireland and the USA are republics today: countries with no king or queen.

items.prompt: How many consuls were elected each year to lead the Roman Republic?
items.explain: Two consuls, each able to block the other, so no single man could become a king again.
items.hook: **Two** consuls, and either could block the other by saying **veto**, Latin for “I forbid”.

items.prompt: What did the letters SPQR, carried on Roman standards, stand for?
items.answer: the Senate and People of Rome
items.explain: Senatus Populusque Romanus: power came from the Senate and the people together.
items.hook: **S**enatus **P**opulus**q**ue **R**omanus: the -que on the end means “and”.
items.example: SPQR is still stamped on drain covers and public buildings in Rome today.

items.prompt: Who were the plebeians?

options.text: Ordinary citizens, not from the noble families
Enslaved people who worked in the mines
options.feedback: Plebeians were free citizens.

options.text: Priests who served in the temple of Jupiter
options.feedback: Plebeians were the ordinary citizens.

items.explain: The long “Conflict of the Orders” won plebeians more rights, including their own officials, the tribunes.
items.hook: **Patricians** comes from pater, father: the noble “fathers”. **Plebs** were the common people.

items.prompt: Which Carthaginian general crossed the Alps with war elephants in 218 BC?
items.explain: Hannibal won great victories in Italy, but Rome finally defeated Carthage in the Punic Wars.
items.hook: Hannibal took **elephants** over the **Alps** in **218 BC**: the most surprising route into Italy imaginable.
items.example: The ruins of Carthage, Hannibal’s city, lie near Tunis, the capital of Tunisia.

items.prompt: In 49 BC Julius Caesar led his army across the River Rubicon into Italy, breaking Roman law. Why do we still say “crossing the Rubicon”?

options.text: It means passing a point of no return
It means winning a battle easily
options.feedback: Caesar knew there was no going back: it meant civil war.

options.text: It means making peace
options.feedback: It started a civil war.

items.explain: Bringing an army into Italy was treason, so Caesar had to win or be destroyed.
items.hook: “**The die is cast**”: the words Caesar is said to have spoken as he crossed the Rubicon in 49 BC.

items.prompt: On which date was Julius Caesar assassinated by senators?
items.explain: About sixty senators, led by Brutus and Cassius, stabbed him in the Senate, claiming to save the Republic.
items.hook: “Beware the **Ides of March**”: the 15th of March, made famous by Shakespeare’s play Julius Caesar.

items.prompt: Caesar’s great-nephew Octavian became Rome’s first emperor in 27 BC. Which name did he take?
items.explain: He kept the Senate but held the real power: the Republic had become an empire.
items.hook: **Augustus** = “revered one”: Octavian took the title in **27 BC** and became the first emperor.
items.example: Look at a calendar: July is named after Julius Caesar and August after Augustus.

items.prompt: The Romans worshipped Greek gods under new names. What did they call Athena?
items.explain: Zeus became Jupiter, Hera Juno, Aphrodite Venus, Artemis Diana, Ares Mars and Athena Minerva.
items.hook: Greek → Roman: Zeus → Jupiter, Hera → Juno, Athena → **Minerva**, Ares → Mars.
items.example: The planets Jupiter, Mars, Venus and Mercury all carry the names of Roman gods.

items.prompt: What was the main reason the Roman Republic collapsed in the first century BC?

options.text: Generals with loyal private armies fought for control
Rome was conquered by its old rival Carthage in a long war
options.feedback: Carthage had been destroyed in 146 BC.

options.text: The people voted to bring back a king
options.feedback: Romans hated the word “king”; Augustus avoided it.

items.explain: Marius, Sulla, Pompey and Caesar showed that whoever had the loyal army had the power.
items.hook: **Marius, Sulla, Pompey, Caesar**: four generals whose loyal armies made them stronger than the Senate.

items.prompt: Read the interpretation, then answer: Explain why the Roman Republic became an empire. Use the interpretation and your own knowledge.
hints: Say whether you agree with the interpretation, and why
A clear opening answer to the question
Generals with personal armies (Marius, Sulla, Caesar)
Civil wars and Caesar crossing the Rubicon
How Augustus kept the look of the Republic but held the power
A conclusion naming the most important reason
items.model: The Republic became an empire mainly because generals gained armies that were loyal to them rather than to Rome. Soldiers depended on their general for pay and land, so men like Sulla and Caesar could march on Rome itself. When Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BC, the result was civil war, and the Senate could not stop him becoming dictator. His murder in 44 BC did not save the Republic: it led to more civil war. Octavian won it, and in 27 BC, as Augustus, he kept the Senate and the old titles but held the real power. The most important reason was the private armies, because without them no single man could have overpowered the Republic’s system of two consuls and a Senate. So the interpretation is too simple: Caesar finished the Republic off, but the system of private armies had already broken it.
items.passage: Rome’s Republic did not die of old age. It was murdered by one man’s ambition. Julius Caesar wanted absolute power, crossed the Rubicon to seize it and made himself dictator for life. Without Caesar, the Republic would have survived.
items.passageSource: An interpretation written for this app

items.prompt: Which pope called for the First Crusade at Clermont in 1095?
items.explain: He promised that crusaders’ sins would be forgiven.
items.hook: “**Deus vult!**”, “God wills it!”: the crowd’s cry at Clermont in 1095, according to chroniclers.

items.prompt: In which year did the First Crusade capture Jerusalem?
items.explain: The crusaders took the city after a siege and massacred many of its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants.

items.example: Jerusalem is still a holy city for Jews, Christians and Muslims today.

Faith, and the promise that their sins would be forgiven
options.feedback: This was a powerful motive.

options.text: The chance of land, wealth and adventure

items.explain: Religion, penance, land, wealth and adventure all mattered. Sea routes to India came 400 years later.
items.hook: The three Gs: **God**, **glory** and **gold**: faith, adventure and the hope of land and wealth.

items.prompt: Which Muslim leader recaptured Jerusalem in 1187 after the Battle of Hattin?
items.explain: Saladin (Salah ad-Din) was admired even by his enemies for his mercy when he took the city.
items.hook: **Salah ad-Din** means “righteousness of the faith”. He retook Jerusalem in **1187**.
items.example: A large statue of Saladin on horseback stands in front of the Citadel in Damascus.

items.prompt: How did the Third Crusade (1189–92), led by Richard I, end?

options.text: A truce: Jerusalem stayed Muslim, but pilgrims could visit
Richard captured Jerusalem and was crowned king
options.feedback: He came close but never took it.

options.text: Saladin was killed in battle outside Acre
options.feedback: Saladin died of illness in 1193.

items.explain: Richard the Lionheart and Saladin never met, but they agreed a truce in 1192.
items.hook: **Lion**heart, brave as a lion, yet he spent only about six months of his ten-year reign in England.
items.example: A statue of Richard the Lionheart on horseback stands outside the Houses of Parliament in London.

items.prompt: What did the Fourth Crusade do in 1204?

options.text: It looted Constantinople, a Christian city
It recaptured Jerusalem from the Muslims
options.feedback: It never reached the Holy Land.

options.text: It made a lasting peace with Saladin
options.feedback: Saladin had died in 1193.

items.explain: The sack of Constantinople deeply damaged the Byzantine Empire and relations between Catholic and Orthodox Christians.
items.hook: The **Fourth** Crusade went the wrong way: Christians sacked Christian **Constantinople** in **1204**.
items.example: The four bronze horses of St Mark’s Basilica in Venice were taken from Constantinople in 1204.

items.prompt: The Knights Templar and the Knights Hospitaller were what kind of group?
items.explain: They protected pilgrims and fought in the Holy Land, and grew rich and powerful.
items.hook: The **Templars** took their name from their base by the site of the **Temple** in Jerusalem.
items.example: Temple Church in London was built by the Knights Templar, and the Temple area of London is named after it.

items.prompt: What happened to many Jewish communities in the Rhineland in 1096?

options.text: Crusaders heading east attacked and massacred them
They paid for and led the crusading armies
options.feedback: They were victims of it.

options.text: They were invited to settle in Jerusalem
options.feedback: Crusaders attacked them in Germany.

items.explain: Crusading armies killed thousands of Jews in towns such as Mainz and Worms: a reminder that the crusades brought violence to Europe too.

items.prompt: Which is a long-term consequence of the Crusades?

options.text: More trade and contact between Europe and the Middle East
Christianity disappeared from most of northern and western Europe
options.feedback: It did not.

options.text: The end of all wars fought over religion
options.feedback: Sadly not.

items.explain: Spices, sugar, silk and ideas travelled west, and Italian trading cities like Venice grew rich.
items.hook: Crusaders came home with a taste for **spices, sugar and silk**: trade grew, and Venice grew rich.
items.example: English words such as sugar, syrup and cotton came to us from Arabic.

items.prompt: Read the interpretation, then answer: Explain why so many people went on the First Crusade. Use the interpretation and your own knowledge.
hints: Say whether you agree with the interpretation, and why
A clear opening sentence
Religious reasons: faith, Jerusalem, forgiveness of sins
Other reasons: land, wealth, adventure
The role of Pope Urban II’s speech
A judgement on which reason mattered most
items.model: Tens of thousands joined the First Crusade, mainly for religious reasons. Pope Urban II promised in 1095 that crusaders’ sins would be forgiven, which mattered enormously to people who feared hell. Jerusalem was the holiest place in Christianity, and many believed it was their duty to free it. However, other reasons mattered too. Younger sons of nobles, who would not inherit land, hoped to win estates in the East, and some hoped for wealth or adventure. Urban’s speech was so powerful because it combined these: faith and reward. Overall, religion was the most important reason, because the journey was so dangerous and expensive that only a strong belief would make most people risk it. So I disagree with the interpretation: greed played a part, but faith was the main motive.
items.passage: The crusaders were not really driven by faith. They were land-hungry younger sons and adventurers looking for riches, who used religion as an excuse.
items.passageSource: An interpretation written for this app

England was invaded by a large French army seeking revenge
options.feedback: England had just LOST its French lands.

options.text: The Pope declared war on Henry VI
options.feedback: It was a struggle within the English nobility.

items.explain: Edward IV won the bloody battle of Towton in 1461, perhaps the largest battle ever fought in England.
items.hook: **Towton**, **1461**: fought in a snowstorm on Palm Sunday, it won Edward IV the crown.

They escaped to France and lived there in secret
options.feedback: There is no reliable evidence for that.

options.text: Richard III confessed in writing to having them killed in the Tower
options.feedback: There was no confession.

items.hook: An **unsolved** case: historians can only weigh up the suspects and the evidence.
items.example: Bones found at the Tower of London in 1674 are buried in Westminster Abbey, but were never proved to be the princes.

items.prompt: In which year did Henry Tudor defeat Richard III at the Battle of Bosworth?
items.explain: Richard III was killed, the last English king to die in battle.
items.hook: “A horse! A horse! My kingdom for a horse!”: Shakespeare’s Richard III at Bosworth, **1485**.
items.example: The Bosworth Battlefield Heritage Centre in Leicestershire tells the story of the battle.

items.prompt: What helped Henry Tudor win at Bosworth?

options.text: Sir William Stanley’s men joined Henry at the key moment
Henry had far more cannons, while Richard had none at all
options.feedback: Both sides had some artillery.

options.text: Richard surrendered before the battle began
options.feedback: He died fighting.

items.explain: The Stanleys waited to see who was winning; their intervention was decisive when Richard charged at Henry.
items.hook: The Stanleys sat on the **fence**, then jumped down on Henry’s side.

items.prompt: In 2012, Richard III’s skeleton was found under a car park in which city?
items.explain: DNA from his sister’s living descendants confirmed it. He was reburied in Leicester Cathedral in 2015.
items.hook: A letter **R** (for “reserved”) was painted on the car park near where Richard’s bones were found.
items.example: Richard III was reburied in Leicester Cathedral in 2015, close to where he was found.

items.prompt: Why did Henry VII marry Elizabeth of York in 1486?

options.text: To unite the two houses and strengthen his claim
Because the Pope had ordered the marriage
options.feedback: It was Henry’s own political choice.

options.text: To gain her family’s lands in France
options.feedback: It was about the English crown.

items.explain: The Tudor rose, red and white together, was his symbol of the united houses.
items.hook: Red + white = the **Tudor rose**: Lancaster married York in **1486**.
items.example: Tudor roses are carved all over King’s College Chapel in Cambridge and Hampton Court Palace.

items.prompt: Put these events in order.
items: The Princes in the Tower disappear
items.explain: From a weak king to a new dynasty in about thirty years.
items.hook: **53, 61, 83, 85**: breakdown, Edward, princes, Bosworth: about 30 years from a weak king to a new dynasty.

items.prompt: Read the interpretation, then answer: Why did Henry Tudor win the Battle of Bosworth in 1485? Use the interpretation and your own knowledge.
hints: Say whether you agree with the interpretation, and why
A clear opening answer
Richard III’s unpopularity, including the Princes in the Tower
Help from France and from the Stanleys
Richard’s charge and death
Which reason was most important, and why
items.model: Henry Tudor won mainly because Richard III had lost the trust of powerful nobles. Many suspected Richard of murdering the Princes in the Tower, so some lords would not fight hard for him, and the Earl of Northumberland held his men back. Henry also had French support, which gave him an army to land in Wales. The decisive moment came when Richard charged at Henry himself: Sir William Stanley’s men, who had been watching, attacked Richard, and he was killed. Luck and timing mattered, but the most important reason was Richard’s unpopularity, because it explains why the Stanleys changed sides and why so many of his army did not fight. The interpretation is right that the Stanleys were decisive, but wrong to call it pure luck: their choice reflected Richard’s unpopularity.
items.passage: Henry Tudor won at Bosworth through pure luck. If the Stanleys had stayed out of the battle, Richard III would have won and there would never have been a Tudor dynasty.
items.passageSource: An interpretation written for this app

items.prompt: What does the French word “Renaissance” mean?
items.explain: People believed they were reviving the learning and art of ancient Greece and Rome.
items.hook: **Re** (again) + **naissance** (birth): think of the word renew.
items.example: When an old town or industry comes back to life, newspapers say it is enjoying a renaissance.

items.prompt: In which Italian city did the Renaissance first flourish?
items.explain: Rich, competitive Florence, ruled by the Medici, paid for artists and scholars.
items.hook: **Florence** flowered first: its Latin name, Florentia, means “flourishing”.
items.example: Brunelleschi’s huge red-tiled dome still crowns Florence Cathedral.

items.prompt: Which rich banking family were the great patrons of Florentine art?
items.explain: Patrons paid artists; the Medici funded Botticelli, Michelangelo and many more.
items.hook: The **Medici** were **bankers**: no money, no masterpieces.

items.prompt: Who painted the Mona Lisa and filled notebooks with designs for flying machines?
items.explain: Leonardo was painter, engineer, anatomist and inventor: the “Renaissance man”.
items.hook: **Da Vinci** means “from Vinci”, the small Tuscan town where Leonardo was born in 1452.
items.example: Leonardo’s drawing the Vitruvian Man appears on the Italian one-euro coin.

items.prompt: Who painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in Rome (1508–12)?
items.explain: Contrary to legend, he did not lie on his back: he stood on scaffolding, bending backwards, for four years.
items.hook: **Sistine** comes from Pope **Sixtus** IV, who built the chapel.
items.example: New popes are still chosen in the Sistine Chapel; white smoke from its chimney means a decision has been made.

items.prompt: Who developed the printing press with movable metal type in Mainz in about 1450?
items.explain: His Bible of about 1455 was the first major book printed in Europe with movable type.
items.hook: **Movable type**: single metal letters that could be arranged, inked, printed, then reused.
items.example: Capital letters are called “upper case” because printers kept them in the upper case, or box, of type.

items.prompt: In 1476, William Caxton set up England’s first printing press. Where?
items.explain: Among the first books he printed was Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales.
items.hook: **Caxton**, **1476**, **Westminster**: three words for England’s first printing press.

items.prompt: Which was a result of printing?

options.text: Books became cheaper and ideas spread faster
options.feedback: This helped the Reformation spread.

options.text: Fewer people bothered to learn to read
options.feedback: Literacy rose as books became cheaper.

options.text: Monks copied even more books by hand
options.feedback: Printing replaced hand copying.

items.explain: Luther’s pamphlets were printed in their hundreds of thousands: the Reformation spread on paper.
items.hook: Before print, one book took months to copy; after print, hundreds of copies, so ideas could not be stamped out.

items.prompt: What was Renaissance humanism?

options.text: Studying ancient texts and celebrating human talent

items.model: It was both, but for the people of the Americas it was above all a time of conquest. items.model: Galileo’s ideas alarmed the Church because they challenged its authority to explain the world. Using his telescope, he found evidence that the Earth moves round the Sun, as Copernicus had argued. The Church taught that the Earth was at the centre of God’s creation, and some Bible passages seemed to say the Sun moved. After the Reformation, the Catholic Church was already under attack from Protestants, so it feared that if people could question it about the heavens, they might question its teaching on everything else. items.model: The Great Fire changed London more, even though the plague killed far more people. The plague killed perhaps 100,000 Londoners, a terrible loss, but people kept moving to the city, so the population recovered within a few years and London looked the same. The city was rebuilt with brick and stone instead of timber, with new building rules, and Wren’s St Paul’s and churches still shape the skyline today. items.model: The colonists rebelled mainly because they believed Britain was taking away their rights. After 1763 Parliament taxed them through laws like the Stamp Act and duties on tea, even though they had no MPs, so they argued “no taxation without representation”. Each protest made things worse: after the Boston Tea Party in 1773, Britain closed Boston’s harbour, and in 1775 fighting broke out at Lexington. Enlightenment ideas, like Locke’s natural rights, gave them a way to justify independence, which Jefferson used in 1776. The most important reason was the argument over taxes, because it turned a quarrel about money into a quarrel about freedom. So the revolution won liberty for some colonists, but not the liberty for all that the interpretation claims.

items.model: The Tsar lost power because long-term anger was turned into revolution by the First World War. The war made everything worse: millions of soldiers were killed or wounded, and food and fuel ran short in the cities. Because Nicholas had taken personal command of the army in 1915, he was blamed for the defeats. In February 1917 strikes broke out in Petrograd, and when soldiers refused to fire on the crowds and joined them instead, he had to abdicate. The war mattered most, because it made the old problems unbearable and turned the army against him.
